title: Jain Anekāntavāda — reality seen from many sides
when: Jain tradition links its teachings to Mahāvīra, conventionally dated to the sixth–fifth centuries BCE in North India, though early chronology is uncertain. The method’s roots may be early; its technical vocabulary and systematic forms emerged over centuries, especially in classical Jain philosophy during the first millennium CE. Scholars debate the term’s first attestation.
people: Mahāvīra; Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmin, associated with the Tattvārtha Sūtra; Samantabhadra and Siddhasena Divākara.
origin: Ancient North India’s Jain ascetic communities, followed by debates among Indian philosophical schools.
idea: Anekāntavāda (“many-sidedness”) holds that real things have multiple aspects, so no single description exhausts them. Jain thinkers paired this realism with standpoints (naya) and conditional predication (syādvāda, “in some respect”), showing how apparently conflicting claims may each be true under different conditions—for example, of a thing’s enduring substance versus its changing state. This is not the claim that every opinion is equally valid: statements must specify the aspect or relation they describe. The doctrine developed through debate with other Indian schools.
relevance: It is intellectual humility with teeth: ask what a claim captures, omits, and under which conditions it holds. The method can sharpen disagreement without reducing it to “everyone is right.” It is not generic relativism or a slogan for tolerance, but part of a distinct Jain account of reality and knowledge.
